clue.text: No press gang made Nelson one of these

definitions.text: No press gang made Nelson one of these

parts.words: No press gang made Nelson one of these
parts.note: press gang reads as a body of journalists, and Nelson's statue stands on top of a tall pillar in Trafalgar Square, though no newspaper ever hired him

explanation.surface: A remark that Admiral Nelson was never forcibly recruited by a press gang.
explanation.walkthrough: The press gang suggests naval recruitment, Nelson's world; but the press here is newspapers, and Nelson's Column is the London monument he tops.
explanation.definitionFit: Writers of regular newspaper features are what the press employs, while Nelson only stands on a pillar.

clue.text: Century on which the curtain rises, by no means spineless

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece written on another sits above it

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
the curtain rises on Act I, the opening of a play

explanation.surface: A centenary celebrated as a theatre curtain goes up, the show far from feeble.
explanation.walkthrough: The curtain rises on ACT I of a play.
explanation.definitionFit: Desert succulents bristle with sharp prickles, so they are anything but lacking spines.

clue.text: Floral tributes to frolicsome play by Tottenham

indicators.note: by puts the club's name next to the play word

parts.note: a lark is a bit of fun or a prank
Tottenham Hotspur football club are known as Spurs

explanation.surface: Wreaths sent for a playful game by Tottenham's football team.
explanation.walkthrough: Tottenham Hotspur is a London football club, nicknamed Spurs.
explanation.definitionFit: Delphiniums are garden flowers, so a bunch serves as floral offerings.

clue.text: Time for some lent money to be paid ?

definitions.text: Time for some lent money to be paid ?

parts.words: Time for some lent money to be paid
parts.note: lent reads as the season of Lent: on the Thursday before Easter the monarch hands out special coins to pensioners

explanation.surface: A creditor asking when a loan falls due.
explanation.walkthrough: Maundy money is silver coinage the British monarch gives to elderly people on the Thursday of Holy Week, which falls in Lent.
explanation.definitionFit: The day before Good Friday is when the sovereign distributes royal alms coins.

clue.text: Making first acquaintance with Italian in service

parts.note: an intro is an introduction, meeting someone for the first time
It is the abbreviation for Italian, as in It vermouth

explanation.surface: Meeting an Italian for the first time at church.
explanation.definitionFit: The opening chant sung at the start of a Mass is a part of church worship.

clue.text: Crutched Cratchit

parts.note: the youngest Cratchit child in Dickens's A Christmas Carol walks with a crutch

explanation.walkthrough: In A Christmas Carol, Bob Cratchit's sick little son carries a crutch.
explanation.definitionFit: The small, lame boy of the Cratchit family in Dickens uses a crutch.

clue.text: Just not raining

explanation.definitionFit: Fair means even-handed or just, and fair weather is dry and bright, without rain.

clue.text: Grey as Dame Partlet ?

parts.note: Partlet is the hen in Chaucer's Nun's Priest's Tale

explanation.surface: Comparing a grey colour to the hen of the old fable.
explanation.walkthrough: Dame Partlet is the hen wife of Chanticleer the cockerel in Chaucer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pale and drained of colour, like ash.

clue.text: Crossword compiler having made a howler is a barker

parts.note: anyone caught out in a blunder goes red in the face
a setter compiles crosswords

explanation.surface: A puzzle compiler who blundered gets barked at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'howler' and 'barker' look like dog noises; a howler is a blunder, and the barker is a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: An Irish gun dog breed with a chestnut coat; dogs bark.

clue.text: U-driving ?

parts.note: driving round in a U shape, a full reversal of direction like the military about-face

explanation.definitionFit: A complete about-face of direction, as in a U-shaped manoeuvre on the road.

clue.text: Roundabout for models of sobriety

definitions.meaning: a roundabout route that comes back to its start
'sober as a judge': judges travel a regional court tour of that name

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sober as a judge' is the proverb; English judges traditionally travelled round the assize courts of a region.
explanation.definitionFit: A circuit is a round route, and judges, proverbially sober, travel a circuit of courts.

clue.text: Uttered hoarse negative, so to speak ?

definitions.text: Uttered hoarse negative, so to speak ?

parts.words: Uttered hoarse negative, so to speak
parts.note: hoarse plays on horse: a horse saying 'nay' makes the noise a horse makes, and the past tense of that sound is spoken like 'nayed'

explanation.surface: Someone with a sore throat croaked out a refusal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hoarse' suggests a sore throat; heard as 'horse', and with a 'nay' as the negative, the clue describes a horse's call.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse's whinny is spelt like the word nay with its vowel sound, so a horse saying no makes that call.

clue.text: Batting team no longer batting — what a reverse !

parts.note: in cricket the batting side is said to be in
a side is a team
a dismissed batsman or team is out

explanation.surface: A cricket side that was batting is all out, a sad turnaround.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a team batting is 'in' and one dismissed is 'out'.
explanation.definitionFit: Turned with the lining showing, a garment is completely reversed.

clue.text: With a shake of gin he gets turned on

indicators.note: shaking the drink's letters like a cocktail mixes them into a new order

explanation.surface: A man who gets aroused after a shaken gin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned on' looks like arousal, but it means the thing a door turns on.
explanation.definitionFit: A door swings on its pivot joint, so that fitting is what something is turned on.

clue.text: John like Jack Sprat ?

definitions.meaning: the nursery-rhyme man who ate no fat, so lean and skinny

explanation.walkthrough: John of Gaunt was a 14th-century English prince; Jack Sprat is from an English nursery rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: John of Gaunt was a Plantagenet duke, and Jack Sprat of the nursery rhyme could eat no fat, so was thin.

clue.text: Sort of organs, sir, that don't encourage investment

indicators.note: to sort letters is to arrange them afresh

explanation.surface: A remark to a gentleman about kinds of organ that deter investors.
explanation.walkthrough: Investment is the old military word for besieging a town; troops stationed there resist it.
explanation.definitionFit: Troops guarding a fortress resist being besieged, which is investment in the military sense.

clue.text: He hit on a Shakespearian kettle

definitions.text: He hit on a Shakespearian kettle

parts.words: He hit on a Shakespearian kettle
parts.note: in Hamlet a kettle means a kettledrum, so the man hitting one is an orchestral drummer

explanation.surface: A man who stumbled upon an Elizabethan cooking pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hit on' suggests discovering; it means striking. Hamlet's 'let the kettle to the trumpet speak' uses kettle for kettledrum.
explanation.definitionFit: A player of kettledrums in an orchestra strikes them, and Shakespeare calls the drum a kettle.

clue.text: In metric figures I have concentrated

parts.note: the metric system counts in tens
I've is the contraction

explanation.surface: Someone who has focused hard on metric measurements.
explanation.definitionFit: Intensive farming or study is highly concentrated effort.

clue.text: Concerning origins of the wherewithal

parts.note: re means regarding or about
sources are where things come from

explanation.surface: A query about where someone's money came from.
explanation.definitionFit: Means or funds available are what one needs, the wherewithal.

clue.text: It's France's place to twist Wales's tail

indicators.note: twisting the end of the word turns that stretch the other way round
tail limits the twist to the last pair of letters

parts.note: Cambria is the poetic, Latin name of Wales

explanation.surface: A town in France tweaking the Welsh dragon's tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to twist' acting on 'tail' swaps the last two letters of CAMBRIA, giving AI for IA.
explanation.definitionFit: A town in northern France, site of a famous First World War tank battle.

clue.text: Put in a niche for instance? Check

definitions.text: Put in a niche for instance
definitions.meaning: placed in a recess, i.e. positioned further in from the front
a check is a reversal or hindrance

explanation.definitionFit: Placed in a recess is placed further back, and a check is a reverse or hold-up.

clue.text: Fisher of a northern burn

parts.note: a burn is a Scottish stream, and the fisher is an animal that hunts fish in it

explanation.surface: An angler on a Scottish stream.
explanation.walkthrough: A burn is a Scottish or northern English word for a stream; the fisher is not human but a water mammal.
explanation.definitionFit: This furry river mammal lives by catching fish in streams.

clue.text: New way to smite them in the lists

indicators.note: a fresh arrangement of the word means its letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A knight finds a novel way to strike opponents in the jousting lists.
explanation.walkthrough: The lists suggest a tournament ground for jousting; here they are just lists, whose entries are the 'them'.
explanation.definitionFit: Entries in lists are separate articles or points, each one a single entry.

clue.text: Each quarter has a type of brilliant light

parts.note: E for east, one quarter of the compass
a Very light is a signal flare fired from a pistol

explanation.surface: Every quarter of a town fitted with a bright lamp.
explanation.walkthrough: A Very light is a coloured flare named after its inventor, Edward Very.
explanation.definitionFit: Each and all the others: every one taken singly.

clue.text: Describing Aurora as a wild animal? Tut!

indicators.note: wild suggests the letters run riot into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone tutting at Aurora behaving like a wild beast.
explanation.walkthrough: Aurora is the Roman goddess of the dawn.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means of the morning, so it fits Aurora, goddess of dawn.

clue.text: Rode a toboggan badly glued

indicators.note: badly signals the letters are put together in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A poorly stuck-together sledge was ridden.
explanation.definitionFit: A luge is a racing sledge, so having sledged on one is past tense of riding it.

clue.text: Song that's quite out ?

parts.note: a tune or melody that is entirely outdoors, wide open to the sky

explanation.surface: A tune that is completely out of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quite out' suggests out of date; read as fully outside it describes an outdoor event, and a song is a tune.
explanation.definitionFit: Something outdoors, not under a roof, is fully out in the fresh atmosphere.

clue.text: Wickedness in a face that's mirth-provoking

indicators.note: one word sits within the other word's letters

parts.note: mug is slang for a face
sin is wickedness

explanation.surface: A face showing wickedness that makes people laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: MUG is British slang for a face.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that raises laughter is entertaining or funny.

clue.text: Where to look for the dawn in Scotland

definitions.text: Where to look for the dawn in Scotland

parts.words: Where to look for the dawn in Scotland
parts.note: dawn breaks in the sky to the east, and sky plus E for east names a Hebridean island

explanation.surface: Advice on where to watch the sunrise in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: SKY is where dawn appears and E (east) is where to face; together they name an island of the Inner Hebrides, off Scotland's west coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish island off the west coast, whose name joins the heavens and the east, where dawn comes.

clue.text: Port brings trouble in Jonson to a climax

indicators.note: to adds the final piece after the first, as to a climax
the trouble word sits within the playwright's first name

parts.note: Ben Jonson, the Jacobean playwright
irk means to bother or trouble
things come to a head at a climax

explanation.surface: Something annoying in Ben Jonson's play builds to a climax, said of a port.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Jonson was Shakespeare's contemporary.
explanation.definitionFit: This town on the Wirral opposite Liverpool is a seaport on the Mersey.
